# Placebo effect and blinded trials (`placebo_blinding`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: needs controlled_trial; helped by cognitive_biases
- Core idea: Patients who expect to improve report improvement, and physicians who expect it see it, so a fair test gives the comparison group a sham treatment that looks the same and keeps both patient and assessor ignorant of who received which. If outcomes are similar, the uncertainty around the difference determines how much benefit or harm the comparison can rule out. The classic demonstration is the French royal commission of 1784 on 'animal magnetism': a blindfolded subject had a crisis beside a tree the magnetiser had left untreated. It can be done anywhere with identical flasks numbered by a third person who keeps the key sealed.
- Pitfalls:
  - Overstating the placebo effect: it changes how people feel and report (pain, nausea), it does not shrink tumours or cure infections
  - Mistaking natural recovery and regression to the mean for a placebo effect; only a no-treatment group separates them
  - Blinding the patient but not the person who judges the outcome
  - Exposing a respected healer, relic or exorcist by a sham test humiliates powerful people and can be read as impiety
  - Concluding that the patients were lying; their relief is sincere
- History: europe: 1599 – royal physicians test the supposedly possessed Marthe Brossier with sham holy water and relics; 1784 Franklin, Lavoisier and colleagues test mesmerism with blindfolds; 1799 Haygarth's wooden 'tractors'; 1835 Nuremberg salt test of homeopathy with shuffled, numbered vials; global: 1940s–1950s – double-blind randomised trials become the standard; 1955 Beecher, 'The Powerful Placebo' (its figures are now considered inflated)
- Read:
  - Ted J. Kaptchuk, Intentional Ignorance: A History of Blind Assessment and Placebo Controls in Medicine (1998)
  - John Haygarth, Of the Imagination, as a Cause and as a Cure of Disorders of the Body (1800)
  - Ben Goldacre, Bad Science (2008)
